assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combines new data and quasi-experimental designs with an explanatory framework (tasks, skill-biased change, import competition) for how technology and trade reshape labour demand and wage inequality. Big question, large policy and scholarly influence, and a wide body of follow-on work.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to the task-based approach and the trade-shock work. Hanson is the key partner on the trade-shock design. Katz is a long-standing leader on technology, education and wage structure. Dorn is also a major co-author on the trade-shock papers, so the three-name limit is a real constraint. Acemoglu's overlapping task-model contribution is already recognised.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from roughly the 1990s to the 2010s and has been widely replicated, extended and debated. The recognition timing is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers Dorn over Katz for the trade-shock design.
Overlap with the earlier Goldin and Acemoglu recognitions on technology and inequality.
Persistence and interpretation of the China-shock effects remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Foundational empirical and theoretical work on agglomeration mechanisms, urban growth, housing and the spatial distribution of activity. Establishes causal and microfoundational understanding of why cities exist and thrive, with strong policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Glaeser covers cities, human capital and housing. Duranton and Puga supply the microfoundations of agglomeration (sharing, matching, learning) and the empirical sorting literature. Moretti and Gyourko are also strong, particularly on local labour markets and housing supply. Krugman's earlier prize covers new economic geography, so the credit is partly adjacent.
assessment.maturity: Decades of cumulative work, a mature field, and a robust, replicated evidence base.
uncertainties: Choosing among five strong candidates for three slots.
Distinctness from the Krugman prize on economic geography.
Allocation of credit between the theoretical and empirical strands.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created the law-and-finance research programme linking legal origins, investor protection and financial development. It opened a major comparative field with new cross-country data and a framework that changed how corporate governance and institutions are studied.
assessment.attribution: The LLSV collaboration is a clear, tight trio with seminal joint papers. Vishny is a co-author on important corporate finance work, but the legal-origins core is the three-person team. Shleifer's broader contributions add weight.
assessment.maturity: Seminal papers date from the late 1990s. The literature is mature and has been extensively replicated, revised and criticised.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the legal-origins thesis, including data coding and causal interpretation.
Reputational and conduct controversies around one candidate. Under the scientific-contribution criterion I weigh these only as far as the committee requires.
Overlap with Shleifer's work in other fields complicates how the citation would be framed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. The work includes staggered pricing and contracts, policy rules, and a microfounded normative framework.
assessment.attribution: Calvo (pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the integrated framework) are plausible anchors. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are also major. With eight credited names and a three-person limit, credit is highly contested and any selection omits others who are deserving.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of influence on policy practice and theory.
uncertainties: Very diffuse credit across eight names.
Overlap with prior macro prizes (Lucas, Prescott and Kydland, Sargent and Sims, Phelps).
Debates about the framework's performance after the 2008 and 2020s episodes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Uses new micro-level credit and housing data with credible designs to show how household debt and credit supply drive booms, busts and recessions. This is a strong data-plus-framework contribution with direct policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear, inseparable pair behind the household-leverage view. Campbell's contributions are broader in finance and not specific to this strand.
assessment.maturity: The central work is about 10 to 15 years old, with replication across countries. It is reasonably established, though still younger than the longest-standing candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the evidence base mature enough.
Competing explanations of the 2008 crisis and the relative role of credit supply versus demand.
Overlap with the Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig recognition on banking and crises.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm model changed the theory and empirics of trade by explaining selection, exporter premia and reallocation gains, and it reoriented a large body of firm-level empirical work.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman has long-standing related theoretical work and complementary models of heterogeneous firms. Redding is a leading contributor on quantitative extensions. Bernard, Eaton and Kortum are adjacent but not credited here, so attribution may be incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with a large literature and wide use.
uncertainties: Completeness of credit, given related work by Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum.
Overlap with the earlier Krugman recognition on trade.
Competition for the trade slot from the quantitative Ricardian and Grossman-Helpman candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data used to measure intergenerational mobility and its local determinants. This is a clear case of data discovery combined with credible quasi-experimental designs on a major social question, with substantial influence on empirical practice and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the leading figure. Hendren and Friedman are close co-authors on the mobility and neighbourhood-effect studies. Katz is credited on the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis but is also on another ballot entry. The collaborative, team-based nature of the work makes sharp attribution harder.
assessment.maturity: The work is relatively recent (about 2014 onward), with some strands still being validated, so timing is less mature than for older candidates.
uncertainties: Long-run validation of the neighbourhood-effects findings.
Methodological debates over measurement of mobility and the causal interpretation of place effects.
Chetty also appears in other entries, which complicates how any citation would be framed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM methods are among the most widely used tools in applied microeconomics, macroeconomics and finance, and enable credible estimation with persistent, unobserved heterogeneity. The contribution is a methodological enabler rather than a substantive discovery.
assessment.attribution: Arellano-Bond (1991) and Arellano-Bover and Blundell-Bond (1995, 1998) form a coherent trio. Credit for the underlying ideas is shared with Anderson-Hsiao, Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen, and Chamberlain, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: Mature and thoroughly validated, with weak-instrument and many-instrument concerns well documented.
uncertainties: Whether the committee gives priority to a methods prize this year.
Overlap with GMM and panel-data credit held by others.
Known finite-sample and proliferation-of-instruments weaknesses.
